GTAPViz: Visualizing GTAP Model Results

Pattawee Puangchit

2025-03-02

Source: vignettes/GTAPViz_plot.Rmd
GTAPViz_plot.Rmd

Introduction

This vignette demonstrates how to generate structured, publication-ready figures using GTAPViz’s built-in visualization tools.

The visualization framework is based on the SL4File and HARFile sheets, which define the variables and figure titles used for plotting. Users can specify these directly within an external mapping file or generate them dynamically in the R environment.

Loading Package

Before proceeding, ensure that GTAPViz and HARplus are installed and loaded:

library(GTAPViz)

Note: If the required packages are not yet installed, please refer to:

  • GTAPViz

  • HARplus

Package Overview

This package facilitates the reporting of CGE model outputs, particularly for GTAP users, but it can also be applied to other results based on .har and .sl4 files. Its primary function is to generate Figures and Tables. Additionally, several useful tools are available for data manipulation to enhance figure illustration.

Figure Types {sec:figure-type}

This package introduces four different plot commands that can generate more than 10 different plots:

  1. comparison_plot: Compares a single variable across all experiments for a selected dimension (e.g., region, sector). For example, qgdp, ppriv, and EV can be compared across selected regions (REG).

  2. detail_plot: Provides a comprehensive visualization of a variable across all regions or all sectors within each experiment. For example, qgdp can be plotted across all regions, or qo across all sectors within each country.

  3. macro_plot: Presents global macroeconomic indicators without dimensions, where each experiment is represented by a single aggregated value. Examples include pgdpwld, qgdpwld, and vgdpwld.

  4. stack_plot: Displays the composition of a variable by stacking its components within each experiment, facilitating decomposition analysis. Examples include EV decomposition from GTAP results.

Report Tables

This package provides a single command for generating several pivot tables designed for academic presentations. This vignette provides some examples in Creating Report Table.

  1. Comparison Table
  2. GTAP Macro Table
  3. Detail Table
  4. Decomposition Table

Project Directory

To use this R code, all solution files, including .sl4 and .har, must be saved from RUNGTAP or CMD and placed in the same folder.

Adjust the <project.folder> directory to your desired path. If you maintain the same folder structure as in this code, you may not need to modify the input (<input.folder>), output (<output.folder>), or mapping (<map.folder>) directories.

project.folder <- "your/folder/path"

# Optional: You might not need to adjust this
input.folder <- paste0(project.folder, "/in") 
map.folder <- paste0(project.folder, "/map")      
output.folder <- paste0(project.folder, "/out")

By default, this R code assumes that <project.folder> contains the following three main folders:

  • in – Stores all input files (i.e., .sl4 and .har). See how to name input files for details.
  • map – Stores the mapping .xlsx file (critical for processing). See mapping file
  • out – Stores all exported output files (optional; the function can create it automatically).

Input Folder

All input files must be stored in <input.folder> (default: "/in" inside <project.folder>). To ensure consistency, each .sl4 and .har file must follow the naming format <experiment_name>.sl4 and <experiment_name>-WEL.har. See Input setup for details on “Experiment Names.”

Below is an example of <input.folder>:

Note: You can include as many experiments as needed, but a higher number will increase processing time.

Mapping Folder

The template for the mapping XLSX file is available here: OutputMapping.xlsx. You can specify the variables to extract from solution files in the “SL4File” and HAR file in the “HARFile” sheet. All required variables must be listed in the “Variable” column.

For “Description” and “Unit”, you can define them manually or leave them blank to use GTAPv7 defaults. Note that GTAP defaults apply only to variables included in the GTAPv7 set. If you introduce additional variables, you must define them manually, as no default exists.

Important: “Unit” column is required for all figure commands; without it, the command will not run. “Description” column is optional and can be used as the plot title—concise descriptions are recommended.

You can import your external mapping file into R using the following method:

sl4map <- readxl::read_xlsx(map.folder, sheet = "SL4File")
harmap <- readxl::read_xlsx(map.folder, sheet = "HARFile")

Note: You can name the file whatever you like, but you must adjust the function accordingly. In this vignette, I name the mappings for .sl4 and .har as “sl4map” and “harmap,” respectively.

💡 Tip: The mapping file can also be manually created in R as a dataframe, provided that it follows the exact structure, including column names. The dataframe must contain at least the “Variable” column, while “Description” and “Unit” columns are optional depending on the selected info.mode.

For example, the following R code creates an equivalent mapping dataframe:

mapping_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("qgdp", "EV", "ppriv"),
  Description = c("Real GDP Index", "Welfare Equivalents", "Consumer Price Index"),
  Unit = c("Percent", "million USD", "percent"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

Input Setup

This section defines experiment names, handling of description and unit columns, and output formats for processing GTAP model results.

Experiment Names (<experiment>)

Define the name of your input file in <experiment> to specify the experiment name in the output. While renaming files within R is possible, I highly recommend doing so manually (i.e., aligning with your simulation) before generating plots in R.

For example, specifying the following will automatically process:
- EXP1.sl4 and EXP1-WEL.har
- EXP2.sl4 and EXP2-WEL.har

experiment <- c("EXP1", "EXP2")

💡 Tip: All figures and tables will be sorted based on the order of your input in <experiment>. If you want a specific experiment to appear first, place its name at the beginning when defining <experiment>. See Input Data Preparation for more details.

Important: .har input files must include “-WEL” in their names. See the input folder figure if you are unsure.

Description and Unit Handling (<info.mode>)

Determines how the "Description" and "Unit" columns are included in the output:
- "Yes" → Uses manually defined descriptions and units from the mapping file.
- "No" → Excludes the "Description" and "Unit" columns.
- "GTAPv7" → Uses default definitions and units from GTAP Model Version 7.
- "Mix" → Uses manually defined values where available and GTAP defaults for the rest.

info.mode <- "Mix"

Input Data Preparation

Filtering Data

While all data may be imported, only a subset is typically needed for plotting. Figures cannot display all regions and sectors at once, so this process filters the data to be plotted.

This filtering automation is designed specifically for the GTAP model and works only with the "REG" (Region) and "COMM / ACTS" (Sector) column names. To filter other columns, use data.frame or the dplyr package manually before proceeding with the plot.

GTAP users can specify the regions and sectors to include in the plot below:

selected_regions <- c("USA", "CHN", "CAN", "ASEAN", "ROW")
selected_sector <- NULL

Note: By default, "NULL" includes all, but this may impact plot aesthetics. If the plot appears too dense or visually unclear, consider refining the selection here.

💡 Tip: All figures and tables will be sorted according to the order of your input in <experiment>, <selected_regions>, and <selected_sector>.
For example:
- If selected_regions <- c("USA", "CHN"), the plot for USA will appear before CHN.
- If experiment <- c(EXP2, EXP1), the figure panel for EXP2 will appear before EXP1 (i.e., from left to right).

Automated GTAP Data Processing

To automate the process of generating figures from GTAP results for GTAP users, I have developed a streamlined data extraction method using the HARplus package.

This automation may not work well for non-GTAP models, so you may need to manually extract and manipulate the data before using the figure code provided in this vignette. Refer to manual data processing for more details.

process_gtap_data(
  sl4var = sl4map, 
  harvar = harmap,
  sl4map = sl4map,
  harmap = harmap,
  region_select = selected_regions,
  sector_select = selected_sector,
  subtotal = FALSE,
  experiment = experiment, 
  mapping_info = info.mode,
  project_dir = project.folder,
  plot_data = TRUE,
  output_formats = list(
    "csv" = "No",
    "stata" = "No",
    "rds" = "No",
    "txt" = "No"))

💡 Tip: This automation uses the "HARplus::group_data_by_dims" command. However, other formats, such as "HARplus::get_data_by_var", "HARplus::get_data_by_dims", or your own data format, can also work with the figure code. Keep in mind that these alternatives may require additional data preparation to ensure compatibility with the figure command.

Manual Data Processing

For other models or additional variables that users may want to include in the default model, data can still be prepared in the same format using the following steps:

  1. Use "HARplus::load_sl4x" or "HARplus::load_harx", followed by "HARplus::group_data_by_dims", to obtain the data in the exact same format.

  2. Filter each dataframe using standard R data.frame operations.

  3. Add the "Unit" and "Description" columns (the "Unit" column is required for processing) using the "add_mapping_info" command from this package.

# Step 1: Extracting Data
sl4data1 <- HARplus::load_sl4x(system.file("extdata", "EXP1.sl4", package = "HARplus"))
sl4data2 <- HARplus::load_sl4x(system.file("extdata", "EXP2.sl4", package = "HARplus"))
sl4data <- HARplus::get_data_by_dims(NULL, sl4data1, sl4data2, merge_data = TRUE)

# Step 2: Filtering Data using Dataframe and lapply
manual.data <- lapply(sl4data, function(x) {
  if (is.data.frame(x)) {
    x[x$REG %in% selected_regions & x$COMM %in% selected_sector & x$ACTS %in% selected_sector
      & x$Experiment %in% selected_exp , ]
  } else {
    x  
  }
})

# Step 3: Adding Unit and Description Column
manual.data <- add_mapping_info(manual.data, external_map = "/your/mapping.xlsx",
                                description_info = TRUE,
                                unit_info = TRUE)

Customizing Units and Labels (Optional)

The following two optional processes are recommended for better figure illustration. While they are not mandatory, they are highly recommended.

Note: These processes are not automatically applied in the automation step and must be performed manually.

  1. Converting the default unit column based on your input. For more details, see "?convert_units".
    • Note: You must define the "adjustment" method using /, *, +, or -.
    • Example: To convert values from million USD to billion USD, set adjustment = c("/1000").
  2. Renaming column names for figure generation (e.g., renaming REG to Region) using <HARplus::rename_dims>.
datasets <- list(sl4.plot.data, har.plot.data)

# Convert Unit if Needed
datasets <- lapply(datasets, convert_units,
                   change_unit_from = "million USD",
                   change_unit_to = "billion USD",
                   adjustment = "/1000")

sl4.plot.data <- datasets[[1]]
har.plot.data <- datasets[[2]]

rm(datasets)

Important: Before Starting the Plot

Rule of Thumb

You can modify and rename most columns in the dataframe as long as you adjust the corresponding code accordingly.

However, do NOT rename the columns "Experiment", "Value", or "Variable". While the values inside these columns can be modified freely, their names must remain unchanged.

Key Features to Explore

I highly recommend reviewing the help documentation for each plot command using ?, e.g., ?comparison_plot.

Each function offers multiple customization options and various export methods. Understanding these features will help you fully utilize their capabilities.

Adjusting the following options allows for greater flexibility in visualization:

  • split_by – Specifies the column used to separate plots.

    • Example: Setting "split_by" = "Region" while plotting "x_axis_from" = "Variable" creates a figure for each region containing all variables. Swapping them results in plots for each variable across all regions.

  • separate_figure – Generates individual figures instead of displaying all panels in a single figure. Experimenting with compare_by_experiment and invert_panel can produce various plot styles.

  • color_tone – Controls the base color of the plot for aesthetic consistency. You can specify a color (e.g., "red", "green") or use pre-defined themes included in the package, such as "academic", "economic", "colorblind", "trade", and "purdue".

  • compare_by_experiment – By default, plots are separated by "Experiment". This option allows automatic swapping between "Experiment" and "x_axis_from".

  • invert_panel – Determines which variable is used to create separate panels versus separate plots.

Practical Example

If you have:

  • 3 experiments: Base, Policy1, Policy2
  • 5 regions: USA, EU, China, Japan, Brazil
  • x_axis_from = "Region"
  • split_by = "Variable" (e.g., GDP, Consumption)

Different combinations yield the following results:

compare_by_experiment = FALSE, invert_panel = FALSE

  • Each variable (GDP, Consumption) has a separate plot.
  • Each plot contains 3 panels (one per experiment).
  • The X-axis represents the 5 regions in each panel.

compare_by_experiment = TRUE, invert_panel = FALSE

  • Each variable (GDP, Consumption) has a separate plot.
  • Each plot contains 5 panels (one per region).
  • The X-axis represents the 3 experiments in each panel.

compare_by_experiment = FALSE, invert_panel = TRUE

  • Each experiment (Base, Policy1, Policy2) has a separate plot.
  • Each plot contains panels for each variable (GDP, Consumption).
  • The X-axis represents the regions in each panel.

compare_by_experiment = TRUE, invert_panel = TRUE

  • Each experiment (Base, Policy1, Policy2) has a separate plot.
  • Each plot contains panels for each region.
  • The X-axis represents the variables in each panel.

Comparison Plot

This figure is designed to compare a single dimension across experiments, making it unsuitable for multi-dimensional data. It is primarily used to illustrate comparisons of "Region" across experiments.

You can also use this figure for other single-dimensional comparisons, as long as only one dimension is displayed (e.g., REG, COMM, ACTS).

💡 Tip: To check which data is compatible with this figure, use: "HARplus::group_data_by_dims". Variables listed under the "1D" sublist are suitable for this figure.

For example, plotting qgdp, ppriv, EV, tot, and u will automatically generate six separate figures using the following command:

region.dta <- sl4.plot.data[["1D"]][["Region"]]

comparison_plot(region.dta,
                x_axis_from = "Region",
                split_by = "Variable",
                plot_var = sl4map,
                title_prefix = "Impact on",
                output_dir = output.folder,
                description_as_title = TRUE,
                compare_by_experiment = FALSE,
                invert_panel = FALSE,
                separate_figure = FALSE,
                color_tone = "purdue",
                panel_rows = NULL,
                panel_cols = NULL,
                width = 20,
                height = 12,
                legend_position = "bottom")

💡 Tip: Since the plot does not allow direct font size adjustments, the key to achieving the best figure format is to modify panel_rows/panel_cols and width/height for optimal output. By default, the command automatically calculates a balanced square layout, but I highly recommend experimenting with these settings to refine the result.

GTAP Macro Variable Plot

This figure is designed to display aggregated values for comparison across all experiments, such as global economic impacts. It is specifically intended for GTAP Macro variables extracted from the "Macros" header in <.sl4> files.

Tip: This figure can also be used for other types of aggregated data.

To generate this figure, users must first extract the relevant GTAP Macro variables, if it’s not yet imported, using the <gtap_macros_data> command:

Macros <- gtap_macros_data(
  input_dir = input.folder,
  experiment_names = experiment,
  subtotal_level = FALSE
)

While it’s quite similar process to other variables, the process is a little trickier for GTAP Macros variable since those variables are nested in a single header "Macros" and did not follow your mapping external file automatically.

If you want to specifically only some variables within the GTAP Macros to be plotted as well as to rename those variable, you can do as the follows in R environment:

# Selecting Variables
selected_marcro <- c("pgdpwld", "qgdpwld", "vgdpwld")
macros_new_name <- c("pgdpwld", "qgdpwld", "vgdpwld")

# Rename
macro.map <- data.frame(
  Variable = selected_marcro,
  Description = macros_new_name,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

Tip: This mapping process can also be skipped and used the same .xlsx file to construct like other variables. However, you must define each variable in the "Macros" header manually in the “Variable” column.

To plot this figure, you can use the following command

macro_plot(Macros,
           plot_var = macro.map,
           compare_by_experiment = FALSE,
           color_tone = "grey",
           output_dir = output.folder,
           description_as_title = FALSE,
           panel_rows = 2,
           width = 45,
           separate_figure = FALSE,
           legend_position = "bottom")

Detail Plot

This plot is designed for large-scale data visualization, as implied by its name, <detail_plot>. It illustrates all sectors (COMM or ACTS) or all regions (REG) for each experiment.

This differs from <comparison_plot>, which only visualizes selected regions. Some GTAPv7 variables suitable for this figure include qo, qxw, qmw, pmw, pxw, and qgdp, plotted across all regions within the same experiment.

Since the variable you want to plot may come from different dataframes (i.e., different dimension names), I have developed a function to simplify this process. By selecting "split_by" as the primary column shared across all variables to be plotted, you can specify "y_axis_from" with multiple columns. The function will automatically identify the corresponding column in each dataset.

Another powerful tool is the top_impact option that allows for automatic filtering by selecting only the most affected variables. For example, setting top_impact = 10 will include the top 5 positive and top 5 negative values. If fewer than 5 exist in either category, additional values will be included to meet the specified limit.

For example, in the following code snippet, the function will locate all variables within the dimensions COMM*REG, REG*COMM, ACTS*REG, and REG*ACTS for plotting:

lapply(sl4.plot.data, function(df) {
  detail_plot(df,
              y_axis_from = c("Commodity", "Activity"),
              split_by = "Region",
              plot_var = sl4map,
              output_dir = output.folder,
              description_as_title = TRUE,
              top_impact = 10,
              panel_rows = 1,
              panel_cols = NULL,
              separate_figure = FALSE,
              invert_panel = FALSE,
              width = 50)})

Tip: This figure can include multiple variables on the y-axis, but you may need to manually define the "width" and "height" of the output accordingly.

Decomposition (Stack) Plot

This plot is designed for visualizing decomposition results, allowing users to analyze the contribution of different components to a total value. Unlike <detail_plot>, which visualizes all regions or sectors, <stack_plot> represents the breakdown of a variable across selected categories.

Additionally, this plot provides an option to further decompose the results by unstacking the components instead of displaying them as a stacked bar. This flexibility makes it suitable for analyzing welfare decomposition, trade decomposition, or other GTAP structural breakdowns.

Some GTAPv7 variables that are well-suited for this plot include welfare decomposition components (A), terms of trade decomposition (E1), and other breakdown analyses.

Since decomposition data often involves multiple components, renaming and restructuring the data may be necessary before plotting. For example, the following command renames the "COLUMN" values in the har.plot.data dataframe to provide more meaningful labels for visualization:

# Rename Value if needed
wefare.decomp.rename <- data.frame(
  ColumnName = "COLUMN",
  OldName = c("alloc_A1", "ENDWB1", "tech_C1", "pop_D1", "pref_G1", "tot_E1", "IS_F1"),
  NewName = c("Alloc Eff.", "Endwb", "Tech Chg.", "Pop", "Perf", "ToT", "I-S"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

har.plot.data <- rename_value(har.plot.data, mapping.file = wefare.decomp.rename)
har.plot.data[["A"]][["Variable"]] <- "Welfare"

# Define Decomposition
stack_plot(data = har.plot.data[["A"]],
          x_axis_from = "Region",
          stack_value_from = "COLUMN",
          title_prefix = "",
          output_dir = output.folder,
          separate_figure = FALSE,
          color_tone = "green",
          width = 30,
          height = 15,
          legend_position = "bottom",
          show_total = TRUE,
          unstack_plot = TRUE,
          description_as_title = TRUE)

har.plot.data[["E1"]][["Variable"]] <- "Terms of Trade"

# Define Decomposition
stack_plot(data = har.plot.data[["E1"]],
          x_axis_from = "Region",
          stack_value_from = "PRICES",
          title_prefix = "",
          output_dir = output.folder,
          separate_figure = FALSE,
          color_tone = "green",
          width = 30,
          height = 15,
          legend_position = "bottom",
          show_total = TRUE,
          unstack_plot = TRUE,
          description_as_title = TRUE)

Creating Report Table

This single command generates multiple table formats suitable for academic presentations with minimal adjustments. You can process several data frames in the same code session, even if they require different pivot formats, but each data frame must be defined separately. See the sample code for details.

This vignette shows only a few examples, but for complete usage, consult <?report_table>. Below are key arguments to highlight:

  • pivot_col
    A named list specifying the column to pivot into wide format.
  • group_by
    A list or character vector defining grouping columns.
  • total_column
    If TRUE, adds a “Total” column that sums all numeric columns row-wise.
  • separate_file
    If TRUE, exports each data frame to its own Excel file; otherwise, all go into one workbook.
  • include_units
    If TRUE, retains the “Unit” column in the grouping (recommended).
  • component_exclude
    A vector of component names to exclude (i.e., values in pivot_col that should be omitted).
  • rename_cols
    A named list mapping old column names to new names.
  • var_name_by_description
    If TRUE, names pivoted columns using “Description” (if available).
  • add_var_info
    If TRUE, appends the variable name to its description in parentheses.
  • decimal
    Sets the number of decimal places in output.
  • unit_select
    Keeps only rows matching the specified unit.
  • separate_sheet_by
    Splits the output into multiple sheets by this column.
  • subtotal_level
    If TRUE, applies subtotal-based filtering where applicable.
  • repeat_label
    If TRUE, repeats all labels in every row (i.e., raw dataset style).
  • add_group_line
    Places a border line to separate groups based on the first column.

Note:
- This command works only with the data list format. For instance, you must first convert “GTAPMacro” or any other data frame to a data list (see GTAP Macro Table).
- Variable names in the columns cannot be changed here. To rename them (e.g., country names), do so before invoking this function (see Renaming Values in a Dataframe).

1. Comparison Table 

report_table(
  data_list = sl4.plot.data[["1D"]],
  pivot_col = list(Region = "Variable"),
  group_by =  list(
    Region = list("Experiment", "Region")),
  rename_cols = list("Experiment" = "Scenario"),
  
  total_column = FALSE,
  decimal = 4,
  subtotal_level = FALSE,
  repeat_label = FALSE,
  include_units = TRUE,

  var_name_by_description = FALSE,
  add_var_info = FALSE,
  add_group_line = FALSE,

  separate_sheet_by = NULL,
  export_table = TRUE,
  output_dir = output.folder,
  separate_file = FALSE,
  workbook_name = "comparison"
)

2. GTAP Macro Table 

GTAPMacro <- list(GTAPMacro = Macros)

report_table(
  data_list = GTAPMacro,
  pivot_col = list(
    GTAPMacro = "Experiment"),
  group_by =  list(
    GTAPMacro = list("Variable")),
  rename_cols = list("Experiment" = "Scenario"),
  
  total_column = FALSE,
  decimal = 4,
  subtotal_level = FALSE,
  repeat_label = FALSE,
  include_units = TRUE,

  var_name_by_description = FALSE,
  add_var_info = FALSE,
  add_group_line = FALSE,

  separate_sheet_by = NULL,
  export_table = TRUE,
  output_dir = output.folder,
  separate_file = FALSE,
  workbook_name = "GTAPMacro"
)

3. Detail Table 

report_table(
  data_list = sl4.plot.data[["2D"]],
  
  pivot_col = list(Sector = "Sector"),
  group_by = list(
    Sector = list("Experiment", "Variable", "Region")),
  
  rename_cols = list("Experiment" = "Scenario"),
  
  total_column = FALSE,
  decimal = 6,
  subtotal_level = FALSE,
  repeat_label = FALSE,
  include_units = TRUE,

  var_name_by_description = FALSE,
  add_var_info = FALSE,
  add_group_line = FALSE,

  separate_sheet_by = NULL,
  export_table = TRUE,
  output_dir = output.folder,
  separate_file = FALSE,
  workbook_name = "Detail Table"
)

4. Decomposition Table 

report_table(
  data_list = har.plot.data,
  pivot_col = list(A = "COLUMN", 
                   E1 = "PRICES"),
  group_by = list(
    A = list("Experiment", "REG"), 
    E1 = list("Experiment", "REG", "COMM")
  ),
  rename_cols = list("REG" = "Region", 
                     "COMM" = "Sector",
                     "Experiment" = "Scenario"),
  
  total_column = TRUE,
  decimal = 6,
  subtotal_level = FALSE,
  repeat_label = FALSE,
  include_units = TRUE,

  var_name_by_description = FALSE,
  add_var_info = FALSE,
  add_group_line = FALSE,

  separate_sheet_by = NULL,
  export_table = TRUE,
  output_dir = output.folder,
  separate_file = FALSE,
  workbook_name = "Decomposition"
)

Additional Utilities

1. Adding Unit and Description Columns

If you manually import data or need to adjust the "Description" and "Unit" columns, you can use the following command:

mapping_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("qgdp", "EV", "ppriv"),
  Description = c("Real GDP Index", "Welfare Equivalents", "Consumer Price Index"),
  Unit = c("Percent", "million USD", "percent"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

datasets <- add_mapping_info(mapping_df, external_map = mapping_df, mapping = "Yes")

Note: Use <?add_mapping_info> to understand the meaning of mapping = "Yes", or see Description and Unit Handling for details.

2. Converting Units and Values

GTAP default values are typically reported in million USD, which may be too large for aesthetic plotting. You can use this command to convert units across all variables and data frames.

You can convert all units in the data frame at once, but you must define the order correctly:
- change_unit_from – The original unit name in the "Unit" column that you want to change.
- change_unit_to – The new unit name to be reported in the "Unit" column.
- adjustment – The mathematical operation to convert the old unit to the new one using /, *, +, or -.

For example, you can automate the following conversions:
- Convert million USD to billion USD by dividing the original value by 1,000.
- Convert percent to proportion by dividing the original value by 100.

datasets <- convert_units(change_unit_from = c("million USD", "percent"),
                          change_unit_to = c("billion USD", "proportion"),
                          adjustment = c("/1000", "/100"))

Note: This command has the following limitations:
- The "Unit" column must exist and be named exactly as "Unit". If not, you may need to check the <add_mapping_info> command.
- While the command is case-insensitive (e.g., USD = usd), the spacing structure in unit names must be consistent. For example, the code will not convert "millionUSD" if it is defined as "million USD" with a space.

3. Renaming Columns and Data List Names

If you need to automatically modify column names across all datasets and/or rename data list names simultaneously—such as changing the column name REG to Region or COMM to Commodity—the following command will be useful:

# Creating Mapping File
rename_col <- data.frame(
  old = c("REG", "COMM", "ACTS"),
  new = c("Region", "Commodity", "Activity")
  )

har.plot.data <- HARplus::rename_col(har.plot.data, rename_col)

Tip: You can also create this dataframe for mapping in Excel and import it into the R environment.
Note: The column names must be "old" and "new". See <?HARplus::rename_col> for more details.

4. Renaming Values in a Dataframe

If you need to automatically modify values in any column across the entire dataframe before plotting—such as renaming country names in the REG column (e.g., changing "USA" to "United States" or "CHN" to "China")—the following command will be useful:

rename.region <- data.frame(
  ColumnName = "REG",
  OldName = c("USA", "CHN"),
  NewName = c("United States", "China"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

har.plot.data.rename <- rename_value(har.plot.data, mapping.file = rename.region)

Tip: You can also create this dataframe for mapping in Excel and import it into the R environment.
Note: The column names must be "OldName" and "NewName". The "ColumnName" can be specified directly in the <rename_value> command, as shown in the example: rename_value(data, "REG", mapping.file = "/your/file.xlsx")

Sample Data

Sample data used in this vignette is obtained from the GTAPv7 model and utilizes publicly available data from the GTAP 9 database. For more details, refer to the GTAP Database Archive.
